THOUGHT: The patient is a 55-year-old male with long-standing, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.2%, fasting glucose 142 mg/dL) and heavy smoking history (2 packs/day × 34 years)—both major risk factors for atherosclerosis. His symptoms are highly characteristic of intermittent claudication: exercise-induced calf cramps (especially with treadmill incline), relieved by rest. Crucially, the *tingling pain in the sole upon leg elevation*—worsening when the foot is raised above heart level—is a red flag for *ischemic rest pain*, which typically occurs in advanced peripheral artery disease (PAD) when perfusion pressure falls below tissue demand even at rest; elevation further reduces hydrostatic pressure, worsening ischemia. The straight-leg raise test reproducing pallor and tingling strongly supports this—not neurogenic (no back pain, normal ROM, negative SLR for radicular pain), and not diabetic neuropathy alone (which would not be posture-dependent or associated with absent pedal pulses). Physical exam confirms hemodynamically significant PAD: absent right dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses, while femoral pulses remain palpable—localizing stenosis distal to the femoral bifurcation. Doppler ultrasound confirms *femoropopliteal stenosis*, consistent with the clinical localization. Hypertension (170/92 mm Hg) and smoking further accelerate atherosclerotic progression. While diabetic neuropathy may coexist, the *postural exacerbation*, *absent pulses*, *exercise-limiting claudication*, and *imaging-confirmed stenosis* point to PAD as the primary, unifying diagnosis driving both claudication and ischemic rest pain.

DIAGNOSIS: Critical limb ischemia (CLI) — specifically, right lower extremity due to femoropopliteal artery stenosis.
